title: DRAFT: Reading a PSD and a spectrogram from a measured fistula signal
review_status: DRAFT pending review by a domain expert
learning_objectives: Explain what a power spectral density (PSD) shows and what it hides.
Read a spectrogram as power over time and frequency.
Describe how a filter changes what you see without changing the source data.
State why amplitudes from uncalibrated sensors must not be compared across recordings.
rubric: DRAFT rubric pending review by a domain expert. Score what the learner can show from the measured window, not clinical interpretation.

rubric_criteria.title: Reading the plots
rubric_criteria.description: Correctly describes where power sits in frequency and how it changes over time in the chosen window.

rubric_criteria.title: Method awareness
rubric_criteria.description: Explains the effect of window length or a filter on what is shown.

rubric_criteria.title: Limits
rubric_criteria.description: States that sensor units are uncalibrated and that the plots are not a diagnosis.

blocks.title: Learning objectives
blocks.content: By the end you should be able to: explain what a PSD shows and hides; read a spectrogram as power over time and frequency; describe how a filter changes what you see; and say why amplitudes from uncalibrated sensors are not compared across recordings.

blocks.title: What you are looking at
blocks.content: This is a measured FiSaV recording from a radio-cephalic arteriovenous fistula, captured by force sensors on the skin with a concurrent ECG lead. Sensor units are uncalibrated, so compare shapes, timing and frequency content within this recording only.

blocks.title: Open the signal window
blocks.content: Choose a PZT channel and a 5 second window. Look at the waveform, then the Welch PSD, then the spectrogram tab.

blocks.title: Read the PSD
blocks.content: Where is most of the power in this window (which frequency range)? What does the PSD not tell you about when that power occurred?

blocks.title: Read the spectrogram
blocks.content: Describe one pattern in the spectrogram that repeats over time. How does it relate to the heartbeat you can see in the ECG?

blocks.title: Try a filter
blocks.content: In Signal processing tools, apply a band-pass filter and then a 50 Hz notch. Note what changed in the trace and what stayed the same.

blocks.title: State a limit
blocks.content: Give one reason why this window cannot tell you whether the fistula has a stenosis.

blocks.title: Educator debrief
blocks.content: A PSD averages power over the whole window, so it loses timing; the spectrogram trades frequency detail for time detail. Filters only change the displayed copy. None of these plots is a diagnostic test.
